meaning: In Mandarin, 'giving a clock' (送钟 sòng zhōng) sounds like 'attending a funeral' (送终). Wristwatches are less loaded but still avoided by traditional elders.

notes.cn: Avoid entirely for elders and traditional recipients; a watch for a close younger friend is usually fine.
notes.vn: Some families share the Chinese association; avoid for elders.
notes.jp: Clocks are a normal, welcome gift in Japan, e.g. for a new home.

meaning: Sharp items symbolise cutting a relationship in most Asian cultures.

notes.cn: Recipients sometimes 'pay' a coin back to cancel the bad luck.
notes.jp: Avoid for weddings; quality kitchen knives can be fine as a personal gift to a cook.
notes.in: Some families avoid gifting knives; others do not mind.

meaning: In Mandarin, 'sharing a pear' (分梨 fēn lí) sounds like 'separating' (分离).

notes.cn: Never split a pear with a partner or friend; avoid in fruit baskets.
notes.kr: Large Korean pears are a prized, lucky Chuseok gift.

meaning: 'Umbrella' (伞 sǎn) sounds like 'to break apart' (散 sàn) in Mandarin.
Shoes can imply the recipient will 'walk away'. In Korea, giving shoes to a partner is believed to make them leave.

notes.kr: Avoid for a partner; a token coin back from the recipient is sometimes used to 'buy' them instead.
notes.cn: 鞋 (xié) sounds like 邪 (evil) in some dialects.
notes.th: Feet and shoes are considered low; avoid for elders.

meaning: Associated with tears and parting in Korea and China.

notes.kr: Considered a gift that brings sadness.
notes.jp: Handkerchiefs are actually a common return gift in Japan, but white ones can suggest farewell.

meaning: 'Four' (四 sì / shi / sa) sounds like 'death' (死) in Chinese, Japanese and Korean.

notes.cn: Avoid in amounts, sets and quantities.
notes.jp: Also avoid 9 (ku), which sounds like suffering.

meaning: 'Eight' (八 bā) sounds like 'prosper' (发 fā). The luckiest number in Chinese culture.

notes.jp: 8 (八) widens at the bottom, symbolising growth and prosperity (末広がり).

meaning: In Chinese 9 (九 jiǔ) sounds like 'long-lasting'; in Japanese 9 (ku) sounds like 'suffering'.
Japan and Korea favour odd amounts for celebrations (they cannot be split evenly, like a couple). China favours even numbers ('good things come in pairs').

notes.jp: Wedding cash is usually 30,000 or 50,000 yen.
notes.cn: Use even amounts for weddings and happy events.

meaning: In Indian tradition, adding 1 to a round number means the blessing keeps growing and is never 'complete'.

notes.in: Give 101, 501, 1,001 and so on (or 1,100 and 2,100 for larger gifts), often with the coin attached to the envelope.

meaning: Red is the colour of luck, joy and celebration in Chinese, Vietnamese and Indian culture.

notes.kr: Never write a living person's name in red ink; it is used for the deceased.
notes.jp: Red is festive in Japan too (red and white for celebrations), but a red-ink card or red funeral associations are avoided; red-and-white wrapping is safe.

meaning: White is the traditional colour of mourning across much of Asia.

notes.jp: Red-and-white combinations are celebratory; plain white with black is for funerals.
notes.in: Plain white is associated with widowhood and mourning in many Hindu communities.

meaning: Black wrapping or envelopes are associated with death and bad luck.

notes.jp: Black-and-white mizuhiki cords are for funerals only.
notes.in: Black is avoided for auspicious occasions such as Diwali.

meaning: Gold signals wealth and prosperity; yellow was historically imperial in China and is royal in Thailand.

notes.th: Yellow is associated with the King and Monday; very auspicious.
notes.in: Gold and yellow are classic festive colours.

meaning: 'Wearing a green hat' (戴绿帽子) means a man's partner is unfaithful.

notes.cn: Never give a man a green hat.

meaning: White and yellow chrysanthemums are funeral flowers in China, Korea and Japan.

notes.jp: The chrysanthemum is also the imperial emblem; colourful potted mums are fine, white cut stems are for funerals.

meaning: All-white bouquets can read as funeral flowers.

notes.jp: Also avoid potted plants for hospital visits (roots suggest the illness will 'take root').

term: Potted plant for a sick person
meaning: In Japan, a rooted plant implies the illness will 'take root' (nezuku).

notes.jp: Bring cut flowers (not white) or fruit to hospital visits instead.

meaning: The 'king of flowers' symbolises wealth, honour and romance.
Purity and enlightenment in Buddhist and Hindu culture.

notes.jp: Lotus is linked with Buddhist funerals in Japan; use carefully.

meaning: Resilience and hope: plum blossoms bloom in late winter.
Longevity and good fortune; 1,000 paper cranes (senbazuru) carry a wish.
Perseverance and success: the koi swims upstream to become a dragon.
Power, success and imperial authority.
Longevity in Japan, Korea, Vietnam and India; but in Chinese slang 'turtle' can be an insult.

notes.cn: Turtle imagery is fine in feng shui contexts but avoid calling someone a turtle (乌龟).

meaning: In Japan 'fukurō' sounds like 'no hardship'; elsewhere owls can be omens.

notes.in: Associated with Lakshmi in Bengal, but 'owl' is also an insult for foolishness.

meaning: Some believe mirrors attract spirits or 'break' relationships if they crack.

notes.cn: Fine for close friends; avoid for weddings in traditional families.

meaning: 'Book' (书 shū) sounds like 'lose' (输) in Cantonese and Mandarin.

notes.cn: Avoid at Lunar New Year for business owners and anyone who plays mahjong.

meaning: Universally respectful; signals health and refinement.

notes.jp: Green tea is also a common funeral return gift, so a beautifully wrapped celebratory version is best for happy occasions.

meaning: Welcome in East Asia for adults who drink; avoid for Muslim and many Hindu and Jain households.

notes.in: Ask first; many families do not drink.
notes.cn: Pairs of bottles are traditional for elders and in-laws.

meaning: Beef is avoided by most Hindus; pork by Muslims. Always check for Muslim recipients anywhere in Asia.

notes.in: Choose vegetarian gifts unless you know the family's diet.

meaning: Leather comes from cattle, which is sensitive in many Hindu and Jain households.

notes.in: Choose vegan or textile alternatives for traditional families.

meaning: An empty wallet suggests poverty; tuck a note or coin inside.
Sound like 'gold' and 'luck'; the classic Lunar New Year visiting gift.
'Apple' (苹果 píngguǒ) sounds like 'peace' (平安); given on Christmas Eve in China.
Long noodles mean long life; eaten on birthdays and at New Year (toshikoshi soba).
Round like the full moon: family reunion and completeness.
Sweetening the mouth marks every happy occasion in India.
Cash in the right envelope is the expected gift at weddings and New Year across much of Asia.

notes.jp: Use new bills and a noshi-decorated envelope; never a plain envelope.
notes.kr: Use a white envelope for weddings (with a celebratory phrase) and new bills.

meaning: Accepted by younger recipients; can feel impersonal to elders.

notes.jp: For superiors, a physical, wrapped gift is more polite.

meaning: In Japan, giving stationery to a superior can imply 'work harder'.

notes.kr: Never write names in red ink.
notes.cn: A quality pen set is a classic business gift.

meaning: 'Kushi' sounds like 'ku' (suffering) + 'shi' (death).
Protection, purity and longevity.
A store of value and a classic gift for weddings and newborns.

notes.in: Very auspicious around Dhanteras and Akshaya Tritiya.

meaning: 'Good things come in pairs' (好事成双) in Chinese culture.

notes.jp: For weddings, even numbers can suggest a split; sets of pairs are fine for couples' items such as matching cups.
